title: Verb and adjective preposition patterns
objectives: Choose prepositions in common verb and adjective patterns.
Use an -ing form after a preposition.
Distinguish listen to from hear with a direct object.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Some English verbs and adjectives are commonly followed by a particular preposition. We say ‘listen to music’, ‘wait for a bus’ and ‘be interested in art’. The preposition connects the first word to a noun, pronoun or -ing form: ‘She is interested in music’ and ‘She is interested in learning music’.

These combinations are useful to learn as whole patterns. A translation from another language may suggest a different preposition, but English has its own established combinations. Context matters because the same word can have more than one pattern or meaning.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Common verb patterns include listen to someone or something, wait for someone or something, depend on someone or something, belong to someone, and pay for something: ‘We waited for the bus’ and ‘This book belongs to Ana’. Pay can also have other patterns, including pay someone for something: ‘I paid the driver for the journey’.

Common adjective patterns include good at an activity, interested in a subject, afraid of something, responsible for something and proud of someone or something. A form of be often comes before the adjective: ‘He is good at chess’ and ‘They are responsible for the project’. The subject of be agrees with the person or thing described.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: When a verb follows a preposition in these patterns, it normally takes an -ing form: ‘She is good at solving puzzles’, ‘I am interested in learning Spanish’ and ‘Thank you for helping’. Here in, at and for are prepositions, so the next verb has -ing in these examples.

Compare ‘listen to music’ with ‘hear music’. Listen focuses on paying attention and normally takes to before its object. Hear can directly take an object: ‘I can hear music’. Compare ‘wait for the bus’ with ‘expect the bus’: expect can take a direct object without for in this meaning.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not omit the preposition from the learned pattern: ‘She listens to music’, not ‘She listens music’. Do not add an extra preposition to a direct-object verb: ‘I heard the news’, not ‘I heard to the news’. In ‘good at swimming’, use an -ing form after at rather than a to-infinitive.

A preposition does not always belong exclusively to one word. A person may be ‘good with children’ or ‘good to a friend’, with meanings different from ‘good at chess’. Rather than applying one combination to every situation, learn the word, its preposition and a short example together.

examples.note: Listen to introduces what she pays attention to.
Wait for introduces the thing awaited.

examples.note: Depend on introduces the relevant factor.

examples.note: Good at is followed by an -ing form.

examples.note: Interested in is followed by an -ing form.

examples.note: Responsible for introduces the area of responsibility.
